Inverse trigonometric functions. They recover angles from trigonometric ratios. If sine of theta equals x, then theta equals arcsin of x, also denoted as sine to the minus one of x. Similarly for arccosine and arctangent. Since trigonometric functions are periodic, they are not one-to-one on their natural domains. We restrict to principal ranges, such as negative pi over two to pi over two for arcsin, to define legitimate inverses with single-valued outputs. These functions appear ubiquitously in navigation, physics, engineering, and computer graphics whenever we need to find an angle from a known trigonometric ratio.

Arcsin of x is defined for x in the interval from negative one to one, with range from negative pi over two to pi over two. Arcsin of sine of theta equals theta only if theta is in this principal range. Otherwise the angle must be reduced to this interval. Arccos of x is defined for x in the interval from negative one to one, with range from zero to pi. Note the different principal range reflecting cosine's decreasing monotonicity and symmetry properties. Arctan of x is defined for all real x, with range from negative pi over two to pi over two. It approaches plus or minus pi over two asymptotically as x approaches plus or minus infinity, never quite reaching the limits.

The derivative of arcsin of x is one divided by the square root of one minus x squared. The derivative of arccos of x is negative one divided by the square root of one minus x squared. The derivative of arctan of x is one divided by one plus x squared. These derivatives reveal the function's sensitivity to input changes. These derivatives are critical to integration. The integral of one divided by the square root of one minus x squared equals arcsin of x plus a constant. The integral of one divided by one plus x squared equals arctan of x plus a constant. These antiderivatives arise in countless applications.

Inverse trig functions are commonly denoted sine to the minus one, cosine to the minus one, tangent to the minus one. However, this notation can confuse since one divided by sine of x is the reciprocal, called cosecant, not the inverse function. The international standard ISO eighty thousand-two uses arcsin, arccos, arctan to avoid ambiguity.

Inverse trig functions are used in physics for angle recovery in projectile motion, finding the launch angle from range, in optics through Snell's law, and in oscillatory systems for phase angle determination. In computer graphics and robotics, inverse trig functions compute rotation angles from coordinate transformations, enabling three-dimensional rendering and inverse kinematics calculations. Multivalued inverses exist for all possible angles with a given sine, cosine, or tangent value, but principal values enable function notation and calculus.
